title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: 2D DP where dp[i][j] = LCS length of the first i chars of `a` and first j chars of `b`. Match → 1 + diagonal; otherwise max of top, left.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: given two strings `a` and `b`, return the length of the longest *subsequence* that appears in both. Subsequence means I can drop characters but must preserve order; characters in the subsequence do NOT need to be adjacent in either input."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Subsequence vs substring — confirming it's subsequence (non-contiguous OK).
• Case-sensitive? ('A' vs 'a' — match or not?)
• Empty inputs — return 0?
• Return value — just the length, or also the subsequence itself?
• Length bounds — `O(m·n)` time/space acceptable?
sections.why: The subsequence-vs-substring clarification is the single most important question — if it were substring (contiguous), this becomes a much different problem solvable in `O(m·n)` with a different recurrence (matches extend a chain, mismatches reset to 0; track the global max). The case-sensitivity question is the everyday clarification that affects the comparison line. Naming the `O(m·n)` upfront preempts the rolling-row optimization discussion.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious exponential solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is recursive: compare the last chars of `a[0..i)` and `b[0..j)`. If they match, recurse on `(i-1, j-1)` and add 1. If they don't, return `max(recurse(i-1, j), recurse(i, j-1))` — drop a char from either side and take the better result. Base case: either prefix empty → return 0. That's `O(2^min(m,n))` worst case because of two-way branching at every mismatch, with heavy overlap on `(i, j)` subproblems. Memoization brings it to `O(m·n)`."
sections.why: The 'match → take diagonal +1, mismatch → max of two predecessors' recursive shape is what plants the recurrence. The bottom-up DP is just memoizing the recursion in reverse, with the table indexed by prefix lengths. The 'no replace op' is the structural difference from Edit Distance — LCS only has two operations on a mismatch (drop from `a` or drop from `b`), not three.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to 2D bottom-up tabulation?
sections.say:
"This is 2D DP over prefix pairs, very close cousin of Edit Distance. The recurrence: `dp[i][j]` = LCS length of `a[0..i)` and `b[0..j)`. The decision at each step is *whether the last chars match*:
• If `a[i-1] === b[j-1]`, the matching pair extends the LCS by one: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`. The +1 says 'I'm taking these two matched chars and chaining them onto the LCS of the smaller prefixes'.
• If they don't match, take the better of dropping one char from either side: `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. The two predecessors are 'drop `a`'s last char' (top) and 'drop `b`'s last char' (left).

Base cases: row 0 and column 0 are zeros — LCS with an empty string is 0, which is what `Array.fill(0)` already gives us. Answer at `dp[m][n]`."
sections.why: Articulating the recurrence as 'match adds 1 to the diagonal; mismatch picks the better of two drops' is the load-bearing pedagogy. The contrast with Edit Distance is the easy distinction: Edit Distance has three mismatch predecessors (delete/insert/replace), LCS has two (drop-from-a / drop-from-b). The 'zeros are already the base case' observation is a nice efficiency — no explicit row/column init, the `fill(0)` does it for free.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — partial overlap, zero overlap, and the case where the common subsequence isn't contiguous in either string.

examples.note: LCS is 'ace' — chars from 'abcde' are at indices 0,2,4 (non-contiguous), but 'ace' itself is the whole of b.
No shared character — every cell mismatches and inherits max(0,0)=0 from the all-zero base row/col. The table stays all zeros.
examples.trace:
init dp (4×4), all zeros.
Row i=1 ('a'): every j mismatches, each cell = max(0, 0) = 0
Row i=2 ('b'): same, all zeros
Row i=3 ('c'): same, all zeros
Final dp = all zeros
return dp[3][3] = 0

examples.note: LCS is 'abc' — sits entirely in the prefix of 'abcba'. The trailing 'ba' doesn't help.

sections.why: Tracing surfaces three things. (1) The 'abcde/ace' case shows the diagonal +1 fires only on actual matches and the max propagates them rightward — that's how non-contiguous matches still compose. (2) The disjoint 'abc/def' case validates the all-zero base: no init needed beyond `fill(0)`. (3) The 'abcba/abc' case shows the LCS doesn't have to live at the end of either string — the answer is reached at dp[3][3] and just gets carried through to dp[5][3].

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Either input empty — `dp[0][n]` or `dp[m][0]` is 0 from `fill(0)`; loop body never executes for that dimension; returns 0. ✓
• Identical strings — every cell on the main diagonal matches and extends, giving `dp[m][m] = m`. The max-of-neighbors also picks up that value through the table.
• Completely disjoint strings — no match ever fires; every cell stays 0 via the max-of-zeros recurrence. Returns 0.
• `a === b` reversed (e.g. "abc" vs "cba") — LCS is 1 (any single shared char wins). The DP handles it without modification.
• Very long inputs — `O(m·n)` time and space; for `m·n > 10^7` consider the rolling-row optimization (`O(min(m,n))` space).
• Unicode — `a[i]` indexes UTF-16 code units; same emoji concern as Edit Distance. Use `[...a]` if needed."
sections.why: The identical-strings and disjoint-strings cases give two easy sanity checks the interviewer can verify mentally. The 'reversed' case is the gotcha — most candidates assume the LCS will be 'large' for similar-looking strings, but the order constraint means anagrams collapse to LCS of 1 unless they happen to share a prefix. Calling it out shows you understand the order-preservation requirement is what distinguishes subsequence from multiset intersection.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is `O(m·n)` — `(m+1)(n+1)` cells, constant work per cell (one comparison, two lookups for the max, or one lookup for the diagonal). Space is `O(m·n)` for the full table.

Space optimization: each cell only reads the previous row (top, diagonal) and the current row (left), so two rolling rows of length `n+1` suffice — drops space to `O(min(m,n))` by making the smaller dimension the inner loop.

Recovering the actual subsequence (not just length) — add backpointers: each cell records whether it came from the diagonal (match), top (drop-`a`), or left (drop-`b`). Walk back from `dp[m][n]`; on each diagonal step append the matched char (in reverse), then reverse at the end. Still `O(m·n)` time and space.

Template family: Edit Distance (same 2D shape, min instead of max, three mismatch predecessors instead of two); Shortest Common Supersequence (`m + n − LCS(a, b)` directly); Longest Palindromic Subsequence (LCS of `s` with `reverse(s)`); Delete Operation for Two Strings (`m + n − 2·LCS`). LCS is the kernel of many string DP problems — solve it once cleanly and the variants are small twists."
sections.why: Naming the rolling-row optimization unprompted is the standard 'can you reduce space?' rebuttal. The 'LCS as a kernel' insight is the senior signal — recognizing that Longest Palindromic Subsequence and Shortest Common Supersequence both reduce to LCS in one transformation is what separates engineers who memorize problems from engineers who see the template family. That insight pays off across every subsequence/edit-style problem you'll see.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the (m+1)×(n+1) LCS table (row 0 / column 0 stay 0). On a character match, dp[i][j] extends the diagonal by 1; on a mismatch, take the better of dropping a char from either string.

reference.approach: 2D tabulation over prefix pairs — diagonal +1 on a match
notes: Row 0 and column 0 stay at 0 — LCS with the empty prefix is 0, so no explicit init needed beyond `fill(0)`.
On a match the diagonal carries +1; on a mismatch take max of the two adjacent cells (drop one char from either side).
Subsequence (order preserved, characters not necessarily adjacent) — distinct from substring, which requires contiguity.
reference.crux: dp[i][j] over prefix pairs: when last chars match, 1 + diagonal; when they don't, max(top, left) — drop a char from either string and keep the better.
cruxDistractors: On a mismatch, reset dp[i][j] to 0 and track a global max — that solves longest common SUBSTRING (contiguous), not subsequence.
Build a frequency map of each string and sum the per-character minimums — counts shared multiset size but ignores the order-preservation constraint.
Greedily walk both strings with two pointers, advancing both on a match and the lexicographically smaller one otherwise.

alternates.label: 1D rolling array (O(min(m,n)) space)
alternates.when: Reach for this when memory is the constraint — the full 2D table is O(m*n) but each row only reads the row above it. A single row of length n+1 plus one saved diagonal value suffices. Make the shorter string the columns to minimize the array.
notes: prev is the completed previous row; curr builds the current row — only O(n) space instead of O(m*n).
prev[j-1] (the diagonal) is safely read before curr[j] overwrites it because j increments left-to-right.
Swapping a and b so the shorter string is columns is optional but halves memory when the strings have very different lengths.

options: LCS length of a[:i] and b[:j]
questions.explain: i and j are prefix LENGTHS, not positions — which is why the comparison is `a[i-1] === b[j-1]` and why row 0 / column 0 (the empty prefix) stay 0 and need no explicit init.

questions.q: On a character match the recurrence is:
questions.explain: A matching pair can always be appended to the best LCS of BOTH prefixes shortened by one, so the diagonal carries +1. Adding 1 to a neighbour instead double-counts — that neighbour may already have consumed the matched character (`"aa"` vs `"a"` would score 2, not 1). Plain max-of-neighbours is the MISMATCH branch.

questions.q: On a mismatch the recurrence is:
questions.explain: The two last characters differ, so at most one of them can be in the LCS — drop a[i-1] or drop b[j-1] and keep the better result. No +1, because nothing was matched. Resetting to 0 is the longest common SUBSTRING recurrence, not this one.

questions.q: How does LCS differ from longest common substring?
options: Substring matches reset to 0 on a mismatch in a 1D scan; subsequence allows the same DP table but tracks the global max instead of dp[m][n]
Substring requires contiguity; subsequence only preserves order
Subsequence requires contiguity in BOTH strings; substring only requires it in one
They're identical when the strings have no repeated characters
questions.explain: A subsequence keeps relative order but allows gaps — `"ace"` in `"abcde"` scores 3 here. A substring must be contiguous in both strings, which is why its table resets to 0 on a mismatch and the answer is the running max over all cells rather than dp[m][n].
